extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (graduate students and researchers) preparing seminar, conference, or colloquium talks
extracted.subtask_description: Practical advice for preparing and delivering mathematical talks (seminars, conference talks, colloquia), focusing on differences from papers, audience engagement, format choice, narrative structure, and time management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating a talk like a paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat a talk like a paper with all attendant details, technicalities, and formalism; never give a talk consisting solely of transparencies of your research paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such talks are almost impossible for anyone not intimately familiar with your work to follow, because audience members cannot easily refer back to earlier notation or comments as they can in a paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Talks should complement papers with high-level overview
rubrics_metrics.description: A talk should complement a paper by providing a high-level and more informal overview of the same material, especially for standard or routine components of the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the talk to channel attention onto the most interesting components and describe those in more detail; consider explaining how the final proofs were obtained (material usually not in papers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be friendly to non-experts at the start
rubrics_metrics.description: Devote at least the first few minutes to basic examples or background so non-experts are not lost from the beginning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even experts appreciate a review; a correctly organized presentation of background helps the new material flow naturally and be better appreciated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use background material to structure the talk
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize your presentation of background material so that treatment of the new material flows naturally and is more readily appreciated by the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear, structured setup of background can make the motivation and development of new results more obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present a standard proof as a template for a new proof
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove New Theorem Y, first review a proof of Standard Theorem X in the style of Y, then later note that Y repeats steps of X with a few key changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the proof of X visible (blackboard/screen) during the lecture; this often works better and can be faster than skipping X to 'save time.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Different emphasis for specialist vs broad audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: For talks aimed primarily at specialists, it is acceptable to focus primarily on the new results after an introduction; for broader audiences (e.g., colloquia) put effort into motivation and the structure of the talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor depth and motivation to the audience: specialists may already appreciate motivation, while broader audiences need more contextualization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use narrative devices to make talks memorable
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat mathematical talks like performing arts: themes, motifs, plot, and other narrative devices help make the talk memorable and communicate key points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical framings: pose open problems at the start and show progress; describe a mysterious phenomenon and reveal explanations; introduce a surprising result then explain how it can be established; state cryptic slogans that are elucidated over the talk; use a three-act structure (setup, difficulties, solutions). Advanced devices (plot twists, nonlinear storytelling, suspense) are possible but harder to pull off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with open problems or a motivating mystery
rubrics_metrics.description: One effective narrative is to pose one or more open problems at the start and devote the rest of the talk to showing progress on those problems, or to describe a mysterious phenomenon and reveal explanations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This framing helps give the talk a clear through-line and engages curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use initially cryptic slogans or graphics to unify the talk
rubrics_metrics.description: State slogans or show an initially cryptic table/graphic near the start which is elucidated during the talk and makes perfect sense by the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mumford’s sketch of Spec Z[x]; such devices can provide a unifying thread.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-act structure and advanced narrative options
rubrics_metrics.description: A three-act structure (setup, encounter difficulties, present solutions) is effective; more advanced narrative devices like plot twists or nonlinear storytelling can be used if the content supports them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These devices can create suspense or surprise but are harder to implement well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use judicious, clarifying humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a small number of judicious jokes (e.g., exaggerated analogies with images) to make the subject less intimidating, but remove jokes that don't assist in clarifying the talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor should aid explanation, not distract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinion and speculation permitted sparingly
rubrics_metrics.description: You may provide some opinion or speculation (e.g., future directions, insights) in addition to stating results, but do so sparingly and only after you have earned enough credibility ("money in the bank").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's common (though not mandatory) to pose open problems at the end of the talk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare tangential material as ‘deleted scenes’
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare tangential material or expanded details of arguments as 'deleted scenes' to show in response to audience questions or if you have extra time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Backup material demonstrates preparation and allows you to keep the main narrative uncluttered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate audience questions with backup material
rubrics_metrics.description: Being able to anticipate questions and having appropriate backup material shows preparation and good taste, and makes the talk more effective and memorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have extra slides, computations, or proofs ready to present if asked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose format based on strengths and weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three main formats—blackboard (whiteboard), transparencies (overheads), and computer presentations (slides)—each with specific strengths and weaknesses; choose accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider what aspects of your material need flexibility, detail, or animation/graphics when selecting a format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blackboard talks for flexibility and referability
rubrics_metrics.description: Blackboard talks are very flexible and allow nonlinear, adaptable presentations; good lecture halls with plenty of blackboard space let the audience see a large part of the talk at once, aiding follow-up and reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use blackboard when you want to develop ideas step-by-step and keep earlier parts visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparencies for rapid detailed information
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparencies can convey detailed information (tables, computations, graphics) efficiently and rapidly—sometimes too rapidly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If two projectors are available, use both and keep a key transparency with crucial definitions/theorems visible during the main part of the talk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computer presentations for animations and online availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Computer presentations (slides) are excellent for animations, graphics, and 'eye candy'; they are also easily made available online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let the style obscure substance; hypertext/popup features can be useful but need careful planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid approaches often work well
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes a hybrid approach (e.g., transparencies for key details, blackboard for big picture, computer for examples) can be effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also note some venues may lack blackboards or overhead projectors, so design your talk with available equipment in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design slide talks around a summary slide
rubrics_metrics.description: For slide talks, create a summary slide that conveys the key takeaways and organise the rest of the talk as a logical progression toward that summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps preserve narrative structure even in a slide-driven presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice and learn timing; avoid cramming
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice to determine how much material fits a time slot; avoid cramming too much mathematics or running hopelessly over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Move optional parts to the end (or deleted scenes) so they can be dropped if necessary; practice even to an empty room to gauge timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable exceptions for overrun are rare
rubrics_metrics.description: Running over time is generally bad unless your work is exceptionally exciting, which is rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better to under-run or cut optional material than to overrun the allocated slot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be pragmatic about venue constraints and available AV
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for the actual facilities (e.g., some conferences may not have blackboards or overhead projectors); design format/content accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan alternatives (e.g., bring slides if no blackboards) and consider hybrid strategies to adapt.
